turns.text: I still remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I had been told, quietly, that I was named in a rally — accused of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter. I wasn’t there when my name was first shouted, but when I walked through the university gates, students dragged me straight onto the stage. There was no trial, no explanation, just fists and slogans. I had argued with Mao’s daughter about ideas, about history, about how to interpret the world. I did not think that disagreement, even with someone so protected, could be twisted into a crime. What I cannot resolve is the speed with which colleagues and students turned on me — some who had once called me friend, now screaming for my confession. I lived, but I do not fully understand how fear, or faith, or ambition could erase so much decency in a single afternoon.

Researcher: After I returned to Beijing from Shanxi, everything I had known about daily life and work was overturned. The institute where I worked had always been a place of quiet, focused research, but suddenly the halls filled with shouting, slogans, and big-character posters. Instead of experiments or papers, we spent our days reading denunciations and writing accusations. I remember the sense of paralysis — the projects abandoned, the equipment gathering dust, the endless meetings where the only work was to find new targets for criticism.

One image I cannot forget is my elderly mother, forced to leave Beijing and return to her rural hometown, wearing a black sash because of her family background. On the bus, I watched as a Red Guard stopped a young man from giving his seat to an old woman until her “class status” was checked. Even small acts of kindness were suspect. I could not understand how ordinary people — children, neighbors — became so quick to judge and punish. The fear was everywhere, but there was also a strange pride among those suddenly in power. I still feel uneasy remembering the laughter of those workers changing the streetlights at night, so loud and free while the rest of us kept our heads down. I never found a place to appeal for fairness, and I never understood how the world turned upside down so quickly.

RedGuard: When I think back, it’s the hospital action that sticks in my mind. I can still feel the sweat on my palms as we sealed the gates and locked down every entrance, the taste of dust in the air as we marched the director and others out into the street. The placards around their necks swung as they walked, black paint still wet, listing their “crimes.” I remember the bonfire at the intersection — the heat on my face, the smell of burning paper and cloth, the way the flames lit up the faces of those we accused. They stood there for hours, silent except for the director, who tried to shout back until we drowned him out. That night, when I heard the nurse had hanged herself, I felt something twist inside me, but I didn’t know what to call it. We thought we were cleansing the old world, but I still see her face, and I don’t know if what we did was justice or something else entirely.

I remember the smell of fried dough from the little shop just outside our compound, and the way the sun hit the dust on the path as we raced our handmade carts down the slope toward the lake. The world felt so big and safe to me then. I didn’t know what a “struggle session” was, or why adults whispered behind closed doors. I only knew that sometimes, when we went outside the compound, the streets would be filled with shouting and banners, and people with red armbands would wave us away or block the road. I thought the parades were like festivals, just noisier and more serious. 

Sometimes my mother would tell me to keep my little brother close and not talk to strangers. Once, I saw a pile of books burning in a courtyard, and I remember thinking it was strange to burn books instead of wood. I asked my friend why, and he just shrugged and said they were “bad books.” I didn’t understand. At home, life was normal—chores, games, laughter. Looking back, I realize how sheltered I was, and how little I understood about what was happening outside our walls. I still wonder what my parents were really thinking and feeling during those years, and why they never let us see their fear.

The thing I have never made sense of is how I ended up with a life so different from everyone I grew up with, and how fast the world could turn upside down. I remember standing in the army barracks, still a teenager, scrubbing floors until my hands bled, thinking I was lucky just to have enough to eat. Then, out of nowhere, I was handed a form that said I’d be sent to Peking University. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was — I thought maybe I’d be learning about some kind of foreign revolution, or maybe it was a code word for something else. 

When I got to Beijing, I was given a badge and a student ID with the university’s seal. I kept touching them in my pocket, as if someone would come and take them back. I knew I hadn’t earned this the old way — no exam, no competition, just a decision from above. In my village, people said it was like being chosen by the gods. But I also saw the looks from others: some with envy, some with suspicion, even some with contempt. 

I can’t forget how quickly people’s attitudes changed toward me, or how I felt both proud and guilty. My family wrote to me about how the fields were empty, how some old classmates had been sent to far-off places, and how nobody knew what the rules were anymore. I was living in a world of banners and slogans, but I also had real food, a real bed, and a future that wasn’t just endless labor. I still don’t know if I was just lucky, or if I was swept up by something bigger that didn’t care about fairness at all. And I never figured out what it meant to deserve anything in those years.

Moderator: All of your memories reflect the upheaval and confusion that defined the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher, your experiences highlight how quickly social relationships and professional norms were overturned, often through mass mobilization and public denunciations. RedGuard, your account of struggle sessions and suicides is historically accurate—these tragic outcomes were not uncommon during the movement’s most radical phases. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sheltered childhood within a military compound is consistent with how some urban families, especially those with military ties, experienced relative protection and limited understanding of the violence outside. CRBeneficiary, your path to university through recommendation rather than exams reflects the suspension of the traditional higher education system, which prioritized political reliability and class background over academic achievement.

You, Red Guard, describe burning books and parading people with placards, and you say you thought you were cleansing the old world. Did you ever stop to ask yourself what exactly was so dangerous about these “old” ideas and people? I watched students destroy libraries, tear up manuscripts, and force professors to kneel for hours — all in the name of revolution. But who decided which knowledge was poisonous and which was pure? I argued with Mao’s daughter about history, about interpretation, and that alone was enough to mark me. Was it really Mao Zedong’s leadership that justified this, or was it something in you — a hunger for power, a need to belong, or just fear of being next? When you saw the nurse’s death, did you truly believe the world was cleaner, or did you just feel emptier?

Researcher: I hear ProfessorR’s question, and it echoes the confusion I felt every day in those years. Red Guard, you talk about “cleansing” and justice, but what I saw was humiliation and destruction. In my institute, decades of research — careful notes, delicate specimens, even old photographs — were tossed out or burned without anyone asking what value was being destroyed. The so-called “poison” was never defined; it was just whatever the loudest voices pointed at. 

I remember watching a young woman, a neighbor, who had always been quiet and hardworking, forced to stand for hours with a pair of filthy shoes around her neck because her father had once been a teacher. Children, barely teenagers, shouted at her, and adults stood by in silence or with nervous smiles. It was not only knowledge that was trampled, but also the dignity of ordinary people. I kept wondering: Did anyone truly believe this was justice, or were most people simply afraid to be next? I never saw a real standard, only shifting targets and endless fear. 

Red Guard, when you saw the director or the nurse — people you may not have known well — did you ever feel the urge to ask why they were chosen? Or did you simply follow the crowd, trusting that the movement itself was always right?

I didn’t ask why, not at first. When the movement started, it felt like the world was finally giving us — the young, the overlooked, the ones always told to keep quiet — a chance to speak and to act. Mao Zedong’s words were everywhere, painted on walls, shouted from loudspeakers, printed in those little red books we carried everywhere. We believed him when he said the old ideas were rotten, that the past was holding us back. I was swept up by it.

When we got the target lists, I didn’t question them. The hospital insiders handed us names and “crimes,” and we acted. It was easy to believe what everyone around me believed — that these people were obstacles, that their foreign books or their old connections made them dangerous. I remember the feeling of certainty as we blocked the hospital gates, the sense of unity as we shouted slogans together. It was only later, after the nurse died and after I saw the faces of people we’d humiliated, that doubt crept in.

But by then, it was already too late to ask why. If you questioned the movement, you risked becoming a target yourself. I saw that happen — someone hesitated once during a struggle session, and the crowd turned on him. So most of us kept our heads down and followed orders. I can’t say it was justice, but I can’t pretend I was innocent either. For a while, I thought we were making history. Now, I wonder if we just destroyed what made us human.

Hearing you talk about burning books and humiliating people, I feel a strange distance. I remember the fire in the courtyard, but to me it was just another odd thing adults were doing. I never thought about where those books came from or who wrote them. When I asked, I was told not to worry, that these things didn’t concern children. I wonder now — did you ever see us watching from behind the gate, or peeking around corners? Did you ever think about what it was like for those of us who were too young to understand, but old enough to notice the fear and excitement in the air?

You say you felt unity, that you believed Mao Zedong and the slogans. I only saw his face on posters and heard his name shouted in the streets. Inside our compound, we learned the songs and waved the flags, but it was like a game to us. I didn’t know what it really meant to “destroy the old world.” I can’t imagine feeling certain about something so big. Were you ever afraid that all this shouting and burning might be wrong? Or did you only start to worry when you saw someone die? I guess I’m trying to understand how you could be so sure when, to me, everything felt confusing and out of reach.

I listen to all of you talk about certainty, about unity, about the feeling of being swept up. I never felt any of that. In my village, we were always on the outside of the slogans. Even when the loudspeakers played Mao Zedong’s speeches, the words felt distant — like thunder on the other side of the mountains. We were told what to believe, but in reality, we believed in getting through the day, in finding enough to eat, in not being the one picked out for struggle or punishment.

When I arrived at Peking University, I saw the walls covered in posters, the slogans painted everywhere — “Down with the old world!” “Long live Chairman Mao!” There were students who shouted these words with force, but there were also plenty who kept their heads down, eyes fixed on the ground, just waiting for the next order. I watched how quickly people learned to perform loyalty, to say the right things, to hide what they really thought. I learned to do it too, because I knew that one wrong word could send me back to the fields or worse.

I never felt certain about any of it — not the slogans, not the burning, not the endless meetings where we were told who to trust and who to hate. I felt lucky, yes, but also always on edge. I kept my badge close, but I also kept my mouth shut. I never trusted that the rules wouldn’t change again. And I never believed that shouting louder or burning more would really decide who deserved what. For me, the only thing I was sure of was that survival meant adapting, not believing. 

When I hear you talk about “making history,” I want to ask: did you ever think about who was left behind? Did you think the slogans would fill an empty stomach, or repair a burned book, or bring back a life lost in the chaos? Because from where I stood, the slogans never changed the hunger, and the banners never made the future any clearer.

Moderator: Your exchanges reveal the varied realities of the Cultural Revolution—urban intellectuals, rural youth, and Red Guards all experienced the movement differently. ProfessorR and Researcher, your recollections of arbitrary persecution and shifting targets are well-supported by historical records. RedGuard, your admission of initial certainty followed by doubt is consistent with the documented trajectory of many Red Guards, who often began with fervor but later questioned their actions, especially after witnessing violence and tragedy. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sense of confusion and partial awareness reflects the experience of many children, particularly those in protected environments. CRBeneficiary, your skepticism and focus on survival echo the feelings of many rural and working-class people, who often saw the movement as distant from their immediate struggles. The diversity of these perspectives highlights how the Cultural Revolution’s impact depended greatly on one’s social position and local context.
